title: The Huggable, Lovable Walrus
summary: Josh and Chuck profile the walrus: its size and birth weight, the Pacific and Atlantic (and disputed Laptev) populations, its relation to red pandas and seals, tusks used for dominance rather than digging, suction feeding on clams, whiskers, blubber and color change, diving physiology, the mating-season "audition" on ice, a 15-month gestation with delayed implantation, Round Island summering, predators (polar bears, killer whales, humans), Indigenous subsistence hunting, and conservation status. The episode also includes banter about animal videos, a Daily Zeitgeist plug, and a listener email from an eleven-year-old fan.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, a plug for the Daily Zeitgeist appearance, and the choice of walrus as a lighter animal topic written by Jennifer Horton. They tease the walrus calf's birth weight.

segments.title: Walrus origins, species and relatives
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Pacific and Atlantic walrus populations, their geographic isolation, and their relation to red pandas and seals. They note the walrus's name is Danish and its scientific name means tooth-walking sea horse. Walrus size is compared between males and females of each population.

segments.title: Walrus tusks and social behavior
segments.summary: The tusks are overgrown canines used mainly to menace rivals in dominance displays, not for digging or prying shells. Walruses can break ice with them and rest hooked on ice. Males and females live apart except during mating, and the animals can live up to about thirty to forty years.

segments.title: Walrus senses, feeding and suction
segments.summary: Walruses have poor eyesight but a strong sense of smell and hearing, and sensitive whiskers. They blow water to stir up clams and use a piston-like tongue to suck the clams out of their shells. They eat a large share of body weight daily.

segments.title: Blubber, color change, diving and oxygen
segments.summary: Walruses have a thick blubber layer that keeps body temperature near normal in icy water. Blood shifts from the skin to the core, changing skin color. They slow their heart rate and store oxygen in muscle to dive. Warming waters force deeper dives and separate some mothers from calves.

segments.title: Walrus vocalizations, mating and gestation
segments.summary: Pharyngeal sacks act as amplifiers for loud walrus calls. Females gather on ice in groups and males compete vocally and by tusking. Females have about a fifteen-month gestation with delayed implantation, and calves may stay with mothers for one to two years. Young males practice tusking early.

segments.title: Round Island and walrus herd behavior
segments.summary: Males gather in large numbers on Round Island in Alaska each summer for a few weeks. The hosts also discuss the walrus's shaky tie to rocky shore and mention the adults' care for injured or dead members.

segments.title: Predators, hunting, Indigenous subsistence and conservation
segments.summary: Polar bears, killer whales and humans are the main threats. Polar bears cause stampedes, and walruses are hunted by a few Indigenous groups in the US, Canada and Russia. A decline occurred during a ban from the sixties to the nineties. Walrus populations are listed as vulnerable but considered stable.

segments.title: Listener mail from an eleven-year-old fan
segments.summary: A listener writes that he is eleven and enjoys the show. The hosts respond and encourage listeners to get in touch.
